claims.text: Moderate post-deposition annealing will refine the nanoscale grain-boundary structure of the thin films.
Grain-boundary refinement will alleviate long-range internal strain.
Grain-boundary refinement will make the distribution of local magnetic exchange interactions more uniform.
Changes in strain and exchange interactions caused by annealing will reduce transition hysteresis.
Annealed films will retain a substantial magnetocaloric effect.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films have an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited films have relatively coarse microstructuring.
Rapid deposition produces inherent internal strain in the as-deposited films.
The proposed annealing can refine grain boundaries without altering the overall alloy composition.
The proposed annealing can refine grain boundaries without generating secondary phases.
The elevated surface-to-volume ratio of the thin films ensures high heat-exchange rates.
Annealing-induced grain refinement reduces cooperative long-range interactions.
Cooperative long-range interactions cause the sharp and hysteretic character of the magnetostructural transition.
Reducing cooperative long-range interactions moderates the abruptness of the magnetostructural phase change.
Moderating transition abruptness broadens the transition temperature range.
The annealed films will have a smaller hysteresis width than the as-deposited films.
The annealed films will have a broader transition temperature range than the as-deposited films.
Annealing will produce only a moderate shift in peak magnetocaloric entropy change.
The as-deposited thin-film baseline has a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited thin-film baseline has limited heat-exchange rates despite its high surface-to-volume ratio.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that the thin films' elevated surface-to-volume ratio ensures high heat-exchange rates, whereas the baseline states that the same thin-film state has limited heat-exchange rates while also having a high surface-to-volume ratio.

The hypothesis describes retention of the magnetocaloric effect 'in as-deposited' films, but the tested and predicted material is post-deposition annealed and therefore is no longer in the as-deposited state.
